metadata.title: Explorando la relación entre las actitudes ante las ciencias y el rendimiento en PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD-provided PISA 2015 science performance and attitudinal indices aggregated to national (and regional) means for 15-year-old students in grades 7 and higher. The paper reports that PISA scores are scaled to an OECD mean of 500 (SD=100) and that attitude indices are constructed from OECD mean of logit scores with equally weighted country samples, but it does not describe applying student-level complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight procedures. Because the analysis is conducted on country/region mean scores rather than individual student microdata, standard PISA sampling-weight application is not documented. The manuscript also does not report any missing-data handling or imputation strategy, suggesting that the analysis relies on the OECD/INEE released aggregated indices and does not perform additional missingness corrections.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are PISA 2015 science performance and attitudinal indices analyzed at the country/regional aggregated level (national means and Spain regional means), not student-level PV-based achievement outcomes. As a result, the paper does not describe plausible value (PV) combining procedures (e.g., Rubin’s rules) because the analysis is not conducted on PV draws at the individual level. Missing-data handling is also not reported because the study appears to use already scaled and aggregated OECD/INEE indices rather than reprocessing student microdata with explicit missingness rules.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 science literacy national mean scores and attitude indices (SEFISCI, PARTSCI, INTSCI, JOYSCI) for 15-year-old students in grades 7 and higher, aggregated across 72 participating countries and economies. For the within-country analysis, used Spain’s 17 autonomous community regional mean scores for the same PISA 2015 science literacy and attitude indices. The paper does not report additional student-level inclusion/exclusion beyond the OECD/INEE released aggregated indices; it also does not describe explicit missing-data exclusions or imputation at the analysis stage.

main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS regression: significant negative linear relationships for all attitude indices (p < .05); slopes range −41 (SEFISCI) to −88 (JOYSCI). Correlations: PARTSCI with science achievement r = −.73; JOYSCI with INTSCI r = .80. Quantile regression: negative slope almost disappears at higher quantiles; for PARTSCI and JOYSCI, Qrm slopes near zero at high quantiles; Quantile Regression Analysis of Deviance: PARTSCI F = 2.09, p = .035; JOYSCI F = 3.43, p = .0007; SEFISCI F = .53, p = .83; INTSCI F = .88, p = .54.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science literacy national mean the study leveraged science self-efficacy, participation in science activities, interest in broad science topics, and enjoyment of science to model science performance, finding that the overall (mean-based) relationships were unexpectedly negative across countries while high quantiles showed much weaker (near-zero) negative slopes. This indicates that policy efforts should not assume a uniformly positive attitude–achievement link when using aggregated cross-country PISA indices, and that heterogeneity by performance level (quantiles) and index comparability/scaling issues should be considered before drawing broad attitudinal improvement strategies.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science literacy (Spain regional means; 17 regions)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Spearman correlations: SEFISCI vs JOYSCI r = .57; SEFISCI vs science performance r = .61 (positive). OLS regional model: SEFISCI significant positive linear relationship (p < .01) with intercept = 507 and slope = 91; other attitude indices show non-significant associations (e.g., JOYSCI vs science performance p = .1).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science literacy regional mean data for Spain, the study leveraged science self-efficacy, participation in science activities, interest in broad science topics, and enjoyment of science to model science performance, finding that only science self-efficacy was significantly and positively associated with science achievement across regions. This indicates that regional interventions strengthening students’ science self-efficacy may be more promising than broad attitude programs targeting all attitude dimensions equally, while also recognizing that the small number of regions (17) limits precision and generalizability.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 science literacy and four attitude indices (SEFISCI, PARTSCI, INTSCI, JOYSCI) using country-level means across 72 PISA participating countries/economies and Spain’s 17 autonomous communities. Rather than training ML models, it applies bivariate correlations plus Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) and quantile regression to characterize how attitude–achievement relationships vary across the science-performance distribution. Across countries, OLS shows significant negative linear relationships (p < .05) with slopes ranging from −41 (SEFISCI) to −88 (JOYSCI), and PARTSCI correlates strongly negatively with science achievement (r = −.73). Quantile regression indicates that the negative association weakens at higher performance quantiles, with PARTSCI and JOYSCI slopes near zero (Qrm vs OLSrm: PARTSCI F = 2.09, p = .035; JOYSCI F = 3.43, p = .0007). Limitations include ecological inference risk from aggregated means and lack of documented PV/missing-data handling because the analysis uses released aggregated indices rather than student-level PV draws.
